newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lufthansa faces cartel ruling, strike threat.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lufthansa faces cartel ruling, strike threat.

text.p: The German cartel office said on Monday an investigation into Lufthansa AG had concluded the German national carrier was overcharging for tickets on flights between Frankfurt and Berlin.
Lufthansa said it would fight the ruling in court.
The Berlin cartel office in January issued a caution to Lufthansa for charging what it called excessive prices on the route and gave the airline a month to respond.

A cartel office spokesman said the ruling would allow Lufthansa to charge only 10 marks ($6 ) more for a one-way ticket on the Berlin-Frankfurt route than it does on the Munich-Berlin route, where Lufthansa faces stiff competition from Deutsche BA, in which British Airways has a 49 percent stake.

Lufthansa has defended the prices it charges on the Frankfurt-Berlin route, saying they were necessary to cover costs. A roundtrip business-class ticket between Frankfurt and Berlin costs about 160 marks more than the Berlin-Munich route.
The ruling comes a day before the DAG union will end voting on a strike-authorisation ballot by the airline's pilots and flight attendants who are members of the union.

Pilots and flight attendants, demanding a one-year contract and a higher-than-offered wage increase, staged two warning strikes last November and December that cost the airline 32 million marks in lost revenue.
Lufthansa has defied the strike threat among members of its 50,000-plus workforce, saying it would implement the same wage deal for the DAG that it had reached with the OeTV union.
The two-year deal for ground workers covered by OeTV, which was reached last October, calls for workers to receive a one-off payment equal to one-third of a month's base pay.
In addition, the airline said workers would receive a 1.7 percent pay rise in 1998 and a small bonus in cash or stock.
The DAG has demanded the airline offer the one-year deal, a top priority for the union since European laws will allow open competition and force Lufthansa to keep cutting costs.

The airline has said it would seek to rein in costs by as much as 20 percent to meet the growing competition. It would contemplate whether to pull out of the Berlin-Frankfurt route and finding a partner airline to operate the service.

A DAG spokesman said the results of the balloting, which will require at least 70 percent approval for any future strike action, will be released on Wednesday. The DAG board will then meet on Friday to discuss its strategy.
"If the Lufthansa management offers further negotiations, then we would agree to that if there was a new offer on the table," a DAG union official told Reuters.
The union has previously predicted that its members would give overwhelming approval to the strike ballot but officials declined on Monday to provide any estimates.
But the airline's chief executive, Juergen Weber, also warned employees in a recent letter to the staff that a strike could have a devastating effect on the carrier's future.

The president of Vereinigung Cockpit pilots' association, Rolf Rehberg, told Reuters on Monday he believed union members would approve the strike ballot but that talks would soon resume with Lufthansa.

"I am sure that we are going to meet in the next week with the Lufthansa board," Rehberg said. "We Germans do not like to strike that often but we are serious about our position. It's not the amount of money we are more concerned about the length of the contract."
